newsitem.title: USA: U.S. markets re-focus on interest rates, earnings.
newsitem.headline: U.S. markets re-focus on interest rates, earnings.

text.p: With the quadrennial U.S. presidential election out of the way, Wall Street is getting back to devoting full attention to two of its favorite topics, interest rates and corporate earnings.

In the background but not completely forgotten are the investigations of President and Mrs. Clinton over the Whitewater real estate transactions, campaign finance and other issues. While campaign rhetoric has subsided, analysts said those issuses could come back to haunt the financial markets should the Clintons find themselves under siege.

"They (the investigations) only become an issue for the markets if you have a genuine government crisis where the president is so preoccupied with survival that he can't govern effectively," said Thomas Gallagher, who specializes in analyzing political trends for Lehman Brothers.
"We're certainly not there yet and Im'not predicting that we will be," said Gallagher.
Gerard Breitner, president of Excomp Asset Management Inc, said Whitewater is one of several clouds hanging over Clinton in his second term.
"If one of them opens up, and I'm not predicting that it will, I think that could send the market into a nasty slide," Breitner said.

Wednesday, in a post-election comment, Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said there would soon be a new set of hearings looking into questions about how Clinton's Democratic Party had been raising funds.
White House officials said the voters, by returning Clinton to office, showed they were not interested in further investigations.
"Certainly it's not going to be a positive for our markets to have a president under siege, said Stephen Poling, executive vice preisdent of Fortis Advisers.
He said investigations may be a psychological negative but they do not affect the economy or interest rates, so the markets could perform at they would if there were no investigatons.

Poling said with the elections out of the way, "I think we're back to where we have been for some time," namely trying to predict the direction of interest rates and the pace of corporate revenues and earnings.

With signs of a slowing economy reflecting a slowdown in capital spending and a subdued consumer, Poling said talk of a pre-emptive move to raise interest rates by the Federal Reserve has receded. "I'm beginning to hear just as many people talking about rate cuts," he said, adding that they could occur in the first half of 1997.

Poling said growth stocks in general are among the more appealing stock groups now, but cautioned individual companies must be studied carefully. He said financially-related stocks should do well as interest rates fall and in the energy group the oil service sector is still attractive.

Breitner believes the historic record shows U.S. financial markets do well in an election year. He said he is not convinced there is real significance to claims that markets falter in the year after a U.S. president is re-elected.
"The markets have had a great run," he said. "If we stay in the slow growth, low inflation pattern, the markets are going to go higher."
THe Dow Jones industrial average was up 86 to 6167 late Wednesday. The post-election rally was broad-based with twice as many New York Stock Exchange issues advancing as there were declines.
